issues.issue: The parenthetical "(“Agreement”) as further defined below.”" is garbled by a stray quotation mark and promises a definition of "Agreement" that the instrument never supplies. Whether "Agreement" includes the exhibits and successor forms is left to Section 15(vii) rather than settled here.

The sentence that "neither party shall in any event be held liable or accountable for any obligations incurred by either party other than as specified herein" cannot easily be squared with the mutual indemnity in Section 13(i), which makes each party answerable for losses caused by its own acts and omissions. Which of the two governs claims for a party's obligations to third parties is unresolved.

"[T]hose products authorized by COMPANY for sale to DISTRIBUTOR" fixes no list, writing or other means by which authorization is shown, so the content of PRODUCTS floats. Combined with COMPANY's right to eliminate any PRODUCT "for any reason," the subject matter of the agreement is indeterminate.

The definition confines the AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE to "retail grocery store outlet customers only," which cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(a)(i), permitting sales to Kmart and to "specific customers as approved by COMPANY," or with Exhibit B's statement that DISTRIBUTOR may distribute to Kmart. Whether Kmart sales are inside or outside the authorized channel (and so a termination ground under Section 12(iii)(a)) is left open.

"[S]tandards that have developed and are universally accepted and followed in the baking industry" is a vague benchmark, and "universally accepted" sets a threshold no practice plausibly meets. Because failure to follow Good Industry Practice is a termination ground under Section 12(iii)(b), the content of the term matters and is unfixed.

"[S]hall continue for until December 31, 2008" and "or until terminates in accordance with paragraph |2 herein" are grammatically broken, leaving unclear whether the agreement simply expires on that date or continues until terminated. The mechanical errors change the meaning of the term.

The final sentence lets either party terminate on ninety days' written notice after December 31, 2008 without any stated cause, while Section 12(i) permits ninety-day termination only "for good cause" or on a change in COMPANY's business. The two cannot both be given effect.

COMPANY's power to "determine the TERRITORY and AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE" during the term conflicts with Section I(iii) and Exhibit A, which fix TERRITORY by a written designation, and with Section 15(iii), permitting modification only by a written instrument executed by both parties. Whether COMPANY can shrink the territory unilaterally is left unresolved.

"[S]pecific customers as approved by COMPANY" specifies no form or manner of approval, so whether oral approval or course of dealing suffices is open. The enumerated permissions (grocery outlets, Kmart) sit against this open-ended third category.

The in-store services "will consist of, but are not limited to" four listed activities, so the catch-all leaves the scope of the service obligation unbounded beyond the enumerated specifics. What further duties the phrase imports is a matter of construction.

The closing sentence — "DISTRIBUTOR must meet certain other guidelines that the COMPANY may determine in its discretion from time to time" — is an unbounded catch-all appended to two specific prohibitions (wholesaler operations and bid processes). Neither the guidelines nor any notice of them is identified.

The duty to adhere to standards, policies and procedures "as shall from time to time be promulgated, altered, amended or modified by COMPANY" lets COMPANY change DISTRIBUTOR's obligations unilaterally, which conflicts with Section 15(iii) permitting modification only by a written instrument executed by both parties. Which provision controls a policy change is unresolved.

"DISTRIBUTOR shall not sell the PRODUCTS ... to any CUSTOMERS or in any AUTHORIZED CHANNEL OF TRADE other than as stated herein" is mis-drafted: read literally it forbids sales in the very channel the agreement authorizes. The mechanical error changes the meaning of the prohibition.

The flat prohibition on selling to customers and channels listed on Exhibit “B” cannot be squared with the closing paragraph of Exhibit B, which permits DISTRIBUTOR to continue selling to and servicing its existing customers falling within that schedule until further notice. Whether legacy excluded-channel customers are a breach turns on which text controls.

The duty to use "commercially reasonable efforts to resolve any conflicts" is triggered only by sales "in conflict with Paragraph 3(a)(i) above," a paragraph number that does not exist in this agreement (the customer list is Section 3(ii)(a)(i)). The miscitation leaves unclear which sales trigger COMPANY's obligation.

Making COMPANY's decision on customer, channel and geographic disputes "FINAL AND BINDING ON DISTRIBUTOR" sits against Section 12(vii), which contemplates either party bringing "a claim under this Agreement," and Section 15(vi)'s choice of Delaware law. Whether this ousts judicial review of channel-of-trade disputes is a question of the instrument read as a whole.

The unqualified promise that "COMPANY shall deliver the PRODUCTS to DISTRIBUTOR" cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(g), which lets COMPANY cancel any delivery in whole or in part in its sole discretion, cut deliveries and discontinue items without liability. Which text measures a delivery failure is unresolved.

"[A]ny cause beyond its control" is undefined and carries no illustrative list, so the events excusing COMPANY's performance have no boundary. Whether commercial or supply-side causes qualify is left to construction.

The sole-discretion right to cancel deliveries, impose "cuts" and discontinue items without liability contradicts the affirmative delivery obligation in Section 3(ii)(e) and the shipment-scheduling promise in Section 6. Read together the supply obligation may be illusory, and which provision yields is unclear.

COMPANY's "sole discretion (which shall be final, conclusive and binding)" to sell within the TERRITORY to customers other than the CUSTOMERS cannot be squared with the promise in Section 3(ii)(d) to use commercially reasonable efforts to resolve conflicting sales. Whether the discretion swallows the effort obligation is a question for construction.

The unlimited right to inspect "any and all warehouse and equipment" used by DISTRIBUTOR without notice stands against Section 14, which expressly limits COMPANY's access to records to "services performed for COMPANY." Whether the same limitation confines physical inspection of premises shared with other product lines is unaddressed.

"[W]holesome snack products" and products "which may reasonably be deemed as injurious to the sales potential of PRODUCTS" are undefined and set no boundary on the non-compete. Which third-party lines DISTRIBUTOR may carry turns on those terms.

The provision specifically authorizes "all other non-cookie or cake snack products (such as potato chips, pretzels, nuts and meat snacks)" but then declares all Nabisco and Pepperidge Farms products (and their affiliates') competitive and forbidden. The blanket authorization and the blanket ban overlap and contradict each other on their face.

The parties "agree to share in the cost" of electronic data processing equipment without stating any allocation, and the reimbursement promise runs "on such terms and in such amounts as COMPANY reimburses its other DSDD distributors," a measure external to the contract. Both leave the money obligation indeterminate.

"[S]hort dated" is defined circularly as products "whose expiration dates are approaching in the near future," giving the term no operative boundary against the separate 45-day notice trigger. What products COMPANY must help dispose of is therefore unclear.

"[S]uch standards ... as are conducive to maintenance and furtherance of the reputation and sale of the PRODUCTS" states no measurable benchmark for servicing, training or accounting. Because Section 12(iii)(b) makes such failures a termination ground, the vagueness is operative.

The obligation to "assist COMPANY in providing or obtaining information as to the credit standing of itself" is garbled as to whose credit standing and what assistance is required. What DISTRIBUTOR must produce on request is not identifiable from the words.

Denying third-party beneficiary status to any "independent contractor of DISTRIBUTOR" sits against Section 15(ii)(a), which expressly permits subdistributors ("independent distributors") who must execute the Exhibit C undertaking running to COMPANY. Whether a subdistributor has any rights under this Agreement is left in doubt.

The carve-out for "accounts where COMPANY is responsible for accounts receivable (e.g. Kmart)" identifies only one example and no way to determine the rest, so which receivables are COMPANY's risk is open. The "e.g." formulation invites dispute over accounts not named.

The one-way indemnity in favour of COMPANY for claims arising from DISTRIBUTOR's obligations cannot easily be squared with the mutual, reciprocal indemnity in Section 13(i). Which regime governs a claim by a customer or subcontractor is left unresolved.

The computation rests on "the approximate $30,000.00 which COMPANY owes DISTRIBUTOR for various credits," so the credits offset are not fixed, and the date of the underlying claim is garbled ("November [4 2006)"). Whether the payment discharged the whole claimed variance is not determinable from the text.

"[S]uch terms as established by COMPANY from time to time" does not say whether "terms" means price, payment terms, or both, and Section 4(v) separately fixes payment terms. The thirty-day notice right to "change the terms" therefore has an uncertain object.

"[S]hipped from a COMPANY DSD Grocery Distribution Center and a COMPANY Non Grocery (NSD) Distribution Center" uses "and" where "or" is apparently meant, leaving unclear whether the 50-case minimum applies to each center separately or to a combined shipment. The conjunction changes the meaning of the minimum-order requirement.

The provision permits price revision "from time to time upon thirty (30) days written notice" and in the same sentence "the right at any time to issue new price lists and to change the prices." The two halves contradict each other on whether notice is required.

Title passing "absolutely" on delivery to DISTRIBUTOR's warehouse sits against Section 12(vi), under which DISTRIBUTOR grants COMPANY a security interest in all PRODUCTS in its possession with a right of self-help repossession, and Section 12(iv)'s repurchase option. The extent of DISTRIBUTOR's ownership must be worked out from the instrument as a whole.

DISTRIBUTOR is made "responsible for the remaining twenty-five percent (25%)" of an allowance it must pass through in full to the customer, but the clause never says how that 25% is charged, deducted or invoiced. How the split is implemented is not determinable from the words.

The "% operating discount" is left wholly to COMPANY's "sole discretion" and "may vary by product," so the discount that offsets DISTRIBUTOR's handling costs has no floor or ascertainable value. Whether any discount at all is owed is therefore open.

The cash discount is keyed to "designated number of days the COMPANY has allowed in its current credit terms," while Section 4(v) fixes a 1% discount for payment within fifteen (or twenty) days. Which measure governs the discount is not reconciled.

The fixed 1%/fifteen-day discount here cannot be squared with the Cash Discount paragraph, which makes the discount period whatever COMPANY "has allowed in its current credit terms," nor with Section 4's right to change "the terms" on thirty days' notice. Which text sets the discount period is unresolved.

The promise that product elimination "shall not relieve the parties of their obligations under such issued orders" cannot be squared with Section 3(ii)(g), which lets COMPANY cancel any delivery in whole or in part and cut or discontinue items without liability. Whether accepted orders survive a discretionary cancellation is left open.

The statement that the Agreement "may be modified only in accordance with the procedures sét forth herein" sits against Sections 3(ii)(b), 3(ii)(c) and 4(ii), which let COMPANY alter policies, Exhibit B and prices unilaterally, and against Section 15(iii)'s requirement of a signed writing. Which "procedures" are meant is not identified.

The delivery obligation is expressed as availability "on the scheduled delivery date, plus or minus five (5) business days," so the "scheduled delivery date" is not a date at all but a ten-day window. Whether a late delivery within that window breaches anything is unclear.

Rejection is permitted both for nonconformity with the Paragraph 8 guarantee and for failure to meet "any quality; and/or grade requirements agreed to in writing," but the exclusive-remedy sentence covers only "any violation of the guarantee set forth in Paragraph 8." What remedy exists for a quality or grade failure is left unstated.

Claims must be reported "as soo as possible, but no later than 24 hours after becoming aware," a trigger tied to undefined awareness and stated in a garbled phrase, and the clause specifies no consequence for a late report. Whether a claim reported after 24 hours is forfeited is not addressed.
